'''Alex K. Zettl''' (born Oct. 11, 1956) is an American experimental physicist, educator, and inventor.

He is a professor of the Graduate School in Physics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and a Senior Scientist at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]. Zettl is a leading expert in the synthesis, characterization, and application of low dimensional materials. He has synthesized and studied new materials, notably those based on carbon, boron and nitrogen, and has made numerous inventions in the field of electronic materials and nano-electromechanical systems. Zettl and his research team were the first to synthesize boron nitride nanotubes,<ref name="Boron Nitride Nanotubes">{{cite journal |last1=Chopra |first1=Nasreen G. |last2=Luyken |first2=R. ==Early life and education==

Zettl was born in San Francisco, California. He attended Sir Francis Drake High School (now Archie Williams High School), the University of California, Berkeley (A.B. 1978) and the University of California, Los Angeles (M.S. 1980, Ph.D. 1983).  His doctoral field of study was experimental [[condensed matter physics]].  His Ph.D. advisor was Prof. George Grüner.

==Career==

As a graduate student, Zettl closely collaborated with two-time Physics Nobel Laureate [[John Bardeen]].  Bardeen had developed a new theory of macroscopic quantum tunneling of charge density waves, and Zettl performed experiments to test the theory.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grüner |first1=G. |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |last3=Clark |first3=W.G. |last4=Bardeen |first4=John |date=15 December 1981 |title=Field and frequency dependence of charge-density-wave conduction in NbSe<sub>3</sub> |journal=Physical Review B |volume=24 |issue=7247 |pages=7247–7257 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.24.7247}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bardeen |first1=J. |last2=Ben-Jacob |first2=E. |last3=Zettl |first3=A. |last4=Grüner |first4=G. |date=16 August 1982 |title=Current Oscillations and Stability of Charge-Density-Wave Motion in NbSe<sub>3</sub> |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=49 |issue=493 |pages=493–496 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.49.493}}</ref>  After completing his Ph.D., Zettl immediately assumed a faculty position in the Physics Department at the University of California, Berkeley, and has remained there throughout his academic career (Assistant Professor, 1983–86; Associate Professor, 1986–1988; Professor, 1988–2022; Professor of the Graduate School in Physics, 2022–present).

At the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Zettl led the superconductivity program from 1990 to 2002, and the sp2-bonded materials program from 1997 to 2022.  From 2004 to 2014 he directed the [[National Science Foundation]] funded Center of Integrated Nanomechanical Systems.  The Center brought together approximately 25 research teams from four institutions (UC Berkeley, Stanford University, [[California Institute of Technology]], and UC Merced) and fostered highly interdisciplinary nanoelectromechanical research. The center also developed numerous educational outreach programs. From 2013 to 2015 Zettl was co-director (along with Carolyn Bertozzi), and from 2015 to 2022 Director, of the Berkeley Nanosciences and Nanoengineering Institute (BNNI), an umbrella organization for expanding and coordinating Berkeley research and educational activities in nanoscale science and engineering.

Zettl has advised approximately 50 graduate students (including those earning Ph.D. degrees in chemistry, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and materials science), and approximately 40 postdoctoral researchers.

==Selected research accomplishments==

Access to Zettl's 600+ research publications, supplementary materials, and research highlights can be found at https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~jode/index.html.

'''Charge density wave statics and nonlinear dynamics'''

Zettl discovered chaotic response<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sherwin |first1=M. |last2=Hall |first2=R. |last3=Zettl |first3=A. |title= Chaotic ac Conductivity in the Charge-Density-Wave State of (TaSe<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>I |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=53 |issue=1387 |date=1 October 1984|pages=1387–1390 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1387}}</ref> and period doubling routes to chaos<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sherwin |first1=M.S. |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |title=Chaotic response of NbSe<sub>3</sub>: Evidence for a new charge-density-wave phase |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=53 |issue=1387 |date=1 October 1984 |page=1387 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1387}}</ref> in dynamic charge density wave (CDW) systems driven by an rf field, and found that mode locking completely freezes out all internal fluctuations of the collective mode condensate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sherwin |first1=M.S. |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |date=15 October 1985 |title=Complete charge density-wave mode locking and freeze-out of fluctuations in NbSe<sub>3</sub> |journal=Physical Review B |volume=32 |issue=5536(R) |pages=5536–5539 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.32.5536|pmid=9937795 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hall |first1=R.P. |last2=Hundley |first2=M.F. |last3=Zettl |first3=A. |date=2 June 1986 |title=Switching and Phase-Slip Centers in Charge-Density-Wave Conductors |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=56 |issue=2399 |pages=2399–2402 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.2399|pmid=10032976 }}</ref>  He identified phase slip centers as the origin of so-called switching in CDWs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bourne |first1=L.C. |last2=Sherwin |first2=M.S. |last3=Zettl |first3=A. |date=5 May 1986 |title=Elastic Properties of Charge-Density-Wave Conductors: ac-dc Electric |doi=10.1088/1367-2630/aa5912|doi-access=free }}</ref> For the 2D static CDW system TaS<sub>2</sub>, Zettl used cryogenic STM measurements to fully characterize domain structure,<ref |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.66.3040|pmid=10043683 }}</ref> and to contrast bulk CDW parameters determined via x-ray scattering to surface CDW parameters established by STM.<ref name="Surface and Bulk '''Carbon and boron nitride nanotubes and related nanostructures'''

Zettl has performed extensive studies on the mechanical and electronic properties of carbon nanotubes (CNTs).  He created electronic devices from CNTs, including a rectifier<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Philip G. |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |last3=Bando |first3=Hiroshi |last4=Thess |first4=Andreas |last5=Smalley |first5=R. E. |title=Nanotube Nanodevice |journal=Science |date=3 October 1997 |volume=278 |issue=5335 |pages=100–102 |doi=10.1126/science.278.5335.100}}</ref> and chemical sensor.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sahoo |first1=Satyaprakash |last2=Chitturi |first2=Venkateswara Rao |last3=Agarwal |first3=Radhe |last4=Jiang |first4=Jin-Wu |last5=Katiyar |first5=Ram S. |title=Thermal Conductivity of Freestanding Single Wall Carbon Nanotube Sheet by Raman Spectroscopy |journal=ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces |date=26 November 2014 |volume=6 |issue=22 |pages=19958–19965 |doi=10.1021/am505484z|pmid=25350877 }}</ref> From thermal conductivity measurements<ref name="A simple and robust electron">{{cite journal |last1=Collins |first1=Philip G. |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |title=A simple and robust electron beam source from carbon nanotubes |journal=Applied Physics Letters |date=23 September 1996 |volume=69 |issue=13 |pages=1969–1971 |doi=10.1063/1.117638}}</ref> he extracted the linear-T behavior expected from the quantum of thermal conductance.  He created a highly robust CNT-based electron field emission source.<ref name="A simple and robust electron" />  Zettl discovered that CNTs could be stable in a fully collapsed state,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chopra |first1=Nasreen G. |last2=Benedict |first2=Lorin X. |last3=Crespi |first3=Vincent H. |last4=Cohen |first4=Marvin L. |last5=Louie |first5=Steven G. |last6=Zettl |first6=A. |title=Fully collapsed carbon nanotubes |journal=Nature |date=September 1995 |volume=377 |issue=6545 |pages=135–138 |doi=10.1038/377135a0|s2cid=4351651 }}</ref> which led to a refined quantification<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Benedict |first1=Lorin X |last2=Chopra |first2=Nasreen G |last3=Cohen |first3=Marvin L |last4=Zettl |first4=A |last5=Louie |first5=Steven G |last6=Crespi |first6=Vincent H |title=Microscopic determination of the interlayer binding energy in graphite |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |date=April 1998 |volume=286 |issue=5–6 |pages=490–496 |doi=10.1016/S0009-2614(97)01466-8}}</ref> of the interlayer interaction energy in graphite; this important parameter had previously been surprisingly ill-defined experimentally.

Zettl was the first to synthesize boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs),<ref name="Boron Nitride Nanotubes"/> for which (in sharp contrast to CNTs), the electronic and optical properties are relatively insensitive to wall number, diameter, and chirality.  Zettl also found different ways to efficiently synthesize<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Han |first1=Wei-Qiang |last2=Cumings |first2=John |last3=Zettl |first3=Alex |title=Pyrolytically grown arrays of highly aligned B<sub>x</sub>C<sub>y</sub>N<sub>z</sub> nanotubes |journal=Applied Physics Letters |date=30 April 2001 |volume=78 |issue=18 |pages=2769–2771 |doi=10.1063/1.1369620}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cumings |first1=John |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |title=Mass-production of boron nitride double-wall nanotubes and nanococoons |journal=Chemical Physics Letters |date=January 2000 |volume=316 |issue=3–4 |pages=211–216 |doi=10.1016/S0009-2614(99)01277-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Han |first1=Wei-Qiang |last2=Cumings |first2=John |last3=Huang |first3=Xiaosheng '''Nanoelectromechanical systems and advances in transmission electron microscopy'''

Zettl developed the transmission electron microscope (TEM) nanomanipulator,<ref name="Peeling and Sharpening"/><ref name="Low-Friction Nanoscale"/> which allowed electrical and mechanical stimulation of nanoscale samples while they were being imaged inside the TEM.  The nanomanipulator could be configured as a mechanical and/or electrical probe placed with atomic precision, as a scanning tunneling microscope, or as an atomic force microscope with simultaneous force measurement capability.<ref name="Interlayer Forces">{{cite journal |last1=Kis |first1=A. |last2=Jensen |first2=K. |last3=Aloni |first3=S. |last4=Mickelson |first4=W. |last5=Zettl |first5=A. |title=Interlayer Forces and Ultralow Sliding Friction in Multiwalled Carbon Nanotubes |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=11 July 2006 |volume=97 |issue=2 |article-number=025501 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.025501|pmid=16907454 |url=https://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/150109 }}</ref> Zettl used the nanomanipulator to prove that multi-wall CNT were composed of nested concentric cylinders rather than scrolls,<ref name="Low-Friction Nanoscale"/> and he determined the fundamental frictional forces between the cylinders.<ref name="Low-Friction Nanoscale"/><ref name="Interlayer Forces" />  This led to his invention of the rotational nanomotor<ref name="Rotational actuators" /> that employed nanotube bearings.  Other inventions by Zettl that resulted were surface-tension-powered relaxation oscillators,<ref name="Carbon Nanotubes as nanoscale mass conveyers" /> tunable resonators,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jensen |first1=K. |last2=Girit |first2=Ç. |last3=Mickelson |first3=W. |last4=Zettl |first4=A. |title=Tunable Nanoresonators Constructed from Telescoping Nanotubes |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=31 May 2006 |volume=96 |issue=21 |article-number=215503 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.215503|pmid=16803247 }}</ref> nanocrystal-powered linear motors,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Regan |first1=B. C. |last2=Aloni |first2=S. |last3=Jensen |first3=K. |last4=Ritchie |first4=R. O. |last5=Zettl |first5=A. |title=Nanocrystal-Powered Nanomotor |journal=Nano Letters |date=1 September 2005 |volume=5 |issue=9 |pages=1730–1733 |doi=10.1021/nl0510659|pmid=16159214 }}</ref> a fully integrated nanoradio receiver,<ref name="Rotational actuators" /> a nanoballoon actuator,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barzegar |first1=Hamid Reza |last2=Yan |first2=Aiming |last3=Coh |first3=Sinisa |last4=Gracia-Espino |first4=Eduardo |last5=Dunn |first5=Gabriel |last6=Wågberg |first6=Thomas |last7=Louie |first7=Steven G. |last8=Cohen |first8=Marvin L. |last9=Zettl |first9=Alex |title=Electrostatically Driven Nanoballoon Actuator |journal=Nano Letters |date=9 November 2016 |volume=16 |issue=11 |pages=6787–6791 |doi=10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b02394|pmid=27704855 }}</ref> and nano-scale electrical<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cumings |first1=John |last2=Zettl |first2=Alex |title=Resistance of Telescoping Nanotubes |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |date=2002 |volume=633 |pages=227–230 |doi=10.1063/1.1514111}}</ref> and thermal<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=C. W. |last2=Okawa |first2=D. |last3=Garcia |first3=H. |last4=Yuzvinsky |first4=T. D. |last5=Majumdar |first5=A. |last6=Zettl |first6=A. |title=Tunable thermal links |journal=Applied Physics Letters |date=7 May 2007 |volume=90 |issue=19 |page=193114 |doi=10.1063/1.2738187}}</ref> rheostats. Zettl used the nanomanipulator to perform the first electron holography experiments<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cumings |first1=John |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |last3=McCartney |first3=M. R. |author3-link=Martha R. McCartney|last4=Spence |first4=J. C. H. |title=Electron Holography of Field-Emitting Carbon Nanotubes |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=18 January 2002 |volume=88 |issue=5 |article-number=056804 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.056804|pmid=11863765 }}</ref> on nanoscale materials, which quantified quantum mechanical field emission from CNTs.  Using an architecture similar to that of his nanoradio, Zettl created a nanoelectromechanical "balance" which had single atom mass sensitivity, and with which he observed atomic shot noise for the first time.<ref name="An atomic-resolution nanomechanical mass sensor" /> He developed a suspended graphene membrane<ref name="Direct Imaging of Lattice Atoms" /><ref name="Graphene at the edge" /> that allowed for nearly real-time TEM imaging of individual carbon atom dynamics, and other isolated atomic and molecular species.  Zettl's development of the TEM graphene liquid cell<ref name="High-Resolution EM" /> and graphene flow cell<ref name="Graphene-Sealed Flow Cells" /> brought ultra-high-resolution real-time liquid phase imaging to the TEM world.  Zettl also developed nanomechanical biological probes,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Xing |last2=Kis |first2=Andras |last3=Zettl |first3=A. |last4=Bertozzi |first4=Carolyn R. |title=A cell nanoinjector based on carbon nanotubes |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=15 May 2007 |volume=104 |issue=20 |pages=8218–8222 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0700567104|pmid=17485677 |pmc=1895932 |doi-access=free }}</ref> tailored nanopores,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pham |first1=Thang |last2=Gibb |first2=Ashley L. |last3=Li |first3=Zhenglu |last4=Gilbert |first4=S. Matt |last5=Song |first5=Chengyu |last6=Louie |first6=Steven G. |last7=Zettl |first7=Alex |title=Formation and Dynamics of Electron-Irradiation-Induced Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride at Elevated Temperatures |journal=Nano Letters |date=9 November 2016 |volume=16 |issue=11 |pages=7142–7147 |doi=10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b03442|pmid=27685639 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gilbert |first1=S. Matt |last2=Dunn |first2=Gabriel |last3=Azizi |first3=Amin |last4=Pham |first4=Thang |last5=Shevitski |first5=Brian |last6=Dimitrov |first6=Edgar |last7=Liu |first7=Stanley |last8=Aloni |first8=Shaul |last9=Zettl |first9=Alex |title=Fabrication of Subnanometer-Precision Nanopores in Hexagonal Boron Nitride |journal=Scientific Reports |date=8 November 2017 |volume=7 |issue=1 |page=15096 |doi=10.1038/s41598-017-12684-x |doi-access=free|pmid=29118413 |pmc=5678191 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gilbert |first1=S Matt |last2=Pham |first2=Thang |last3=Dogan |first3=Mehmet |last4=Oh |first4=Sehoon |last5=Shevitski |first5=Brian |last6=Schumm |first6=Gabe |last7=Liu |first7=Stanley |last8=Ercius |first8=Peter |last9=Aloni |first9=Shaul |last10=Cohen |first10=Marvin L |last11=Zettl |first11=Alex |title=Alternative stacking sequences in hexagonal boron nitride |journal=2D Materials |date=28 March 2019 |volume=6 |issue=2 |page=021006 |doi=10.1088/2053-1583/ab0e24|arxiv=1810.04814 |s2cid=119216315 }}</ref> and highly efficient wideband graphene-based mechanical energy transducers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Qin |last2=Zettl |first2=A. |title=Electrostatic graphene loudspeaker |journal=Applied Physics Letters |date=3 June 2013 |volume=102 |issue=22 |page=223109 |doi=10.1063/1.4806974|arxiv=1303.2391 |s2cid=29754669 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Qin |last2=Zheng |first2=Jinglin |last3=Onishi |first3=Seita |last4=Crommie |first4=M. F. |last5=Zettl |first5=Alex K. |title=Graphene electrostatic microphone and ultrasonic radio |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=21 July 2015 |volume=112 |issue=29 |pages=8942–8946 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1505800112|pmid=26150483 |pmc=4517232 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

'''Isolation of 1D chains and topological materials'''

In analogy to the isolation of 2D graphene from graphite, Zettl developed a method by which single or few chains of quasi 1D materials could be isolated and studied.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pham |first1=Thang |last2=Oh |first2=Sehoon |last3=Stetz |first3=Patrick |last4=Onishi |first4=Seita |last5=Kisielowski |first5=Christian |last6=Cohen |first6=Marvin L. |last7=Zettl |first7=Alex |title=Torsional instability in the single-chain limit of a transition metal trichalcogenide |journal=Science |date=20 July 2018 |volume=361 |issue=6399 |pages=263–266 |doi=10.1126/science.aat4749|pmid=30026223 |arxiv=1803.02866 |s2cid=49896559 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stonemeyer |first1=Scott |last2=Cain |first2=Jeffrey D. |last3=Oh |first3=Sehoon |last4=Azizi |first4=Amin |last5=Elasha |first5=Malik |last6=Thiel |first6=Markus |last7=Song |first7=Chengyu |last8=Ercius |first8=Peter |last9=Cohen |first9=Marvin L. |last10=Zettl |first10=Alex |title=Stabilization of NbTe3, VTe3, and TiTe3 via Nanotube Encapsulation |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=31 March 2021 |volume=143 |issue=12 |pages=4563–4568 |doi=10.1021/jacs.0c10175|pmid=33258601 |arxiv=2009.10869 |s2cid=221856719 }}</ref>  He did this by synthesizing the materials in the confined (and protective) interior of CNTs and BNNTs. The method has yielded structures unknown in "bulk", with often interesting electronic properties (such as sharp metal-to-insulator transitions<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Meyer |first1=Scott |last2=Pham |first2=Thang |last3=Oh |first3=Sehoon |last4=Ercius |first4=Peter |last5=Kisielowski |first5=Christian |last6=Cohen |first6=Marvin L. |last7=Zettl |first7=Alex |title=Metal-insulator transition in quasi-one-dimensional HfTe 3 in the few-chain limit |journal=Physical Review B |date=9 July 2019 |volume=100 |issue=4 |article-number=041403 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.100.041403|arxiv=1903.00464 |s2cid=118830779 }}</ref>) and non-trivial topological properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pham |first1=Thang |last2=Oh |first2=Sehoon |last3=Stonemeyer |first3=Scott |last4=Shevitski |first4=Brian |last5=Cain |first5=Jeffrey D. |last6=Song |first6=Chengyu |last7=Ercius |first7=Peter |last8=Cohen |first8=Marvin L. |last9=Zettl |first9=Alex |title=Emergence of Topologically Nontrivial Spin-Polarized States in a Segmented Linear Chain |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=20 May 2020 |volume=124 |issue=20 |article-number=206403 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.124.206403|pmid=32501077 |arxiv=2001.06565 |s2cid=210839580 }}</ref>  Atomically precise ultra-narrow nanoribbons<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cain |first1=Jeffrey D. |last2=Oh |first2=Sehoon |last3=Azizi |first3=Amin |last4=Stonemeyer |first4=Scott |last5=Dogan |first5=Mehmet |last6=Thiel |first6=Markus |last7=Ercius |first7=Peter |last8=Cohen |first8=Marvin L. |last9=Zettl |first9=Alex |title=Ultranarrow TaS 2 Nanoribbons |journal=Nano Letters |date=14 April 2021 |volume=21 |issue=7 |pages=3211–3217 |doi=10.1021/acs.nanolett.1c00481|pmid=33818102 |arxiv=2012.05399 |s2cid=233029041 }}</ref> were also created by Zettl via this confined growth method.

'''Liquid electronics'''

Using conducting nanoparticles softly "jammed" at the interface between two immiscible liquids, Zettl constructed electronic devices and "circuitry", thus realizing an effective paradigm for "all liquid electronics".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Popple |first1=Derek |last2=Shekhirev |first2=Mikhail |last3=Dai |first3=Chunhui |last4=Kim |first4=Paul |last5=Wang |first5=Katherine Xiaoxin |last6=Ashby |first6=Paul |last7=Helms |first7=Brett A. |last8=Gogotsi |first8=Yury |last9=Russell |first9=Thomas P. |last10=Zettl |first10=Alex |title=All‐Liquid Reconfigurable Electronics Using Jammed MXene Interfaces |journal=Advanced Materials |date=27 October 2022 |volume=35 |issue=13 |article-number=2208148 |doi=10.1002/adma.202208148|pmid=36302090 |doi-access=free }}</ref>  Such constructs could facilitate easier reconfiguration or complete recycling of constituents once the circuit architecture becomes obsolete.

==Personal life==

Zettl is an outdoor enthusiast.  He is an avid sea and whitewater kayaker and a whitewater rafter.  He has guided numerous whitewater raft trips on class 5 rivers throughout California, and has guided wilderness descents of the Tatshenshini and Alsek Rivers in Alaska and a mid-winter descent of the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon.  Zettl enjoys backcountry skiing and mountaineering, especially expedition climbing.  He has led or co-led numerous climbing expeditions to the Alaska Range, the Saint Elias Range (Alaska and the Yukon), and the Andes of Ecuador, Peru, and Argentina.  He has climbed technical routes on Denali, and completed a ski descent of Mt. Logan, Canada's highest peak.  He has climbed extensively in the Sierra Nevada of California, the Cascades of the Pacific Northwest, the volcanoes of Mexico, the Alps of Germany, France, Switzerland, and Italy, the peaks of Morocco and Tanzania, the Alps of Japan and New Zealand, and in the Himalaya and Karakoram of Nepal and Pakistan.  Zettl also enjoys designing and constructing amateur electronics, and building and operating off-road vehicles.
